name: AI in Prior Authorization
blurb: Automating approvals between providers and payers.
title: AI in Prior Authorization
answer: Prior authorization is a major administrative burden, and AI platforms now review requests against payer policy and approve many automatically. Federal rules are pushing the process onto electronic interfaces with set response times, which makes automation easier.

reading.body:
Prior authorization automation is arriving fastest on the approval side, while automated denials remain the point of legal and clinical scrutiny.

The pattern in the data is a split between what the technology does well and where it is contested. Cohere Health reports its platform can approve up to 90 percent of authorization requests automatically, which is a claim about volume on the approval path. The same data offers no equivalent figure for denials, and the guidance attached to this topic is to keep a clinician on every denial. That asymmetry is the story: approval is a matching problem against written payer policy, and denial is a judgment with consequences that payers and providers have reason to contest.

The regulatory piece explains why this is automatable at all. The CMS interoperability and prior authorization final rule, finalized in January 2024, requires payers to support electronic prior authorization and faster decisions. Set response times and electronic interfaces convert a paper negotiation into a structured transaction, and structured transactions are what software reviews well. Prior authorization has been a major administrative burden precisely because it was unstructured.

What the data does not cover is scale. There is one funding round and one vendor claim, no count of payers running automated review, no error rate, no denial-overturn rate, and no measure of how much clinician time the automation returns. The 90 percent figure is the vendor's own and applies to requests its platform handles, not to prior authorization overall. The compute and power questions that shape the rest of AI do not surface here, because this workload is policy matching over clinical text rather than large-scale training.
